messages.subject: Re: boxplot overlay
messages.body_plain:
> Using the data and code below, I have created two plots that I would
> like to overlay.  The first plot is a "profile" plot, and is meant to
> convey the average salinity values for individual fields tracked
> through time in two different study regions (hence the two colors).
> It may turn out that I need to separate the data, and plot the red and
> blue data in their own graphs.  However, it is the parallel-ness of
> the lines from one sampling event to another that was found to be
> statistically high (the correlation between any two consecutive
> sampling events was found to be approx. equal to 0.8, or in other
> words as a group (red or blue) their values either went collectively
> up, down or remained roughly the same)

To start, I'd recommend using lubridate for date parsing, and making a
plot that captures the essence of your display, without worrying about
all the fiddly details - that's much easier to play around with.
Here's my version:

library(lubridate)

dat.boxplot$Plot_date <- mdy(dat.boxplot$Plot_date)
dat.boxplot$Measurement_Date <- mdy(dat.boxplot$Measurement_Date)

ggplot(dat.boxplot, aes(Measurement_Date, log10(ECe_mean), colour = Region)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Field_Number), alpha =1/4, size = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(Plot_date, group = interaction(Plot_date,Region)))

> 1)  The only question I have for the first plot is this:  Is there way
> to assign different alpha values based on the value of "Region"?

Are you sure you want to?  I don't think this will help the display.

> The second plot gives boxplots meant to summarize, or call attention
> to, each sampling event's summary statistics.  However, there are a
> couple of difficulties with it:
>
> 1)  I need to fix the box width, much like the "width" argument in the
> standard R boxplot command.  I wasn't able to find the answer I was
> looking for at: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_boxplot.html.  How might
> I do this?

It doesn't look like it's possible, due to a bug in geom_boxplot.

> 2)  I tried placing a "fill" command in the second plot, but no matter
> where I tried it, it would work.  Where would I add the fill command
> to play around with filling in the boxes?

You want to map fill to a variable, so you need to add it into the
aesthetic mappings:

ggplot(dat.boxplot, aes(Measurement_Date, log10(ECe_mean))) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Field_Number, colour = Region), alpha =1/4,
size = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(Plot_date, group = interaction(Plot_date,Region),
fill = Region))

> 3)  Is there a way to make the line's of each box thicker?

ggplot(dat.boxplot, aes(Measurement_Date, log10(ECe_mean))) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Field_Number, colour = Region), alpha =1/4,
size = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(Plot_date, group = interaction(Plot_date,Region),
fill = Region), size = 2)

> 4)  Is there something analogous to staplewex (from the standard R
> boxplot function call) in geom_boxplot()?  Again, I could find an
> answer to this from http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_boxplot.html

There isn't an equivalent.

> 5)  How do I overlay the plots?  I strongly suspect it will not look
> good at first, but I'm hoping that through color manipulation, alpha
> manipulation, etc. that it will clean up nicely.

See above.

That said, I think you'd be better off using facetting for this plot:

ggplot(dat.boxplot, aes(Measurement_Date, log10(ECe_mean))) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Field_Number), colour = "grey50", alpha = 1/4) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(Plot_date, group = Plot_date)) +
  facet_grid(Region ~ .)

And

messages.subject: Solved: qqline
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I fiddled around some more and found a solution. Here it is:

>>
p <- ggplot(subset(d.molten, variable%in%c("pcu","pcl","anu","anl")), aes(sample=value))

slope <- function(x){(quantile(x, p=.75)-quantile(x,.25))/(qnorm(.75)-qnorm(.25))}

d.qqline <- cast(d.molten, variable~., fun=function(x){
                 list(slope=slope(x),
                 intercept=quantile(x,.25)-slope(x)*qnorm(.25))},
                 subset=variable%in%c("pcu","pcl","anu","anl"))

pg <- p + geom_point(stat="qq") + facet_wrap(~variable) + theme_bw()

pg + geom_abline(data=d.qqline, aes(intercept=intercept, slope=slope))
<<

Maybe someone can benefit from this.

Best,
Paul

messages.subject_clean: geom_ribbon and when below or above y=0
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I can not find a solution for a rather simple plot, like this one
http://www.cpc.noaa.gov/products/precip/CWlink/pna/month_nao_index.shtml.

The idea is to use geom_ribbon with different colour for values below
with y<0 and y>0.

url <- 'http://www.cpc.noaa.gov/products/precip/CWlink/pna/norm.nao.monthly.b5001.current.ascii'
file  <- tempfile()
download.file(url,file)
nao <- read.table(file, header = F)
names(nao) <- c('Year', 'Month', 'NAO')
nao$Date <- as.Date(paste(nao$Year, nao$Month, '15'), format = "%Y %m %d")
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(nao, aes(Date, ymin = ifelse(NAO>0, 0, NAO))) +
        geom_ribbon(aes(ymax = ifelse(NAO>0, NAO, 0),
                     colour = ifelse(NAO>0, 'red', 'blue'),
                     fill = ifelse(NAO>0, 'red', 'blue')))

This seems to split the data into two parts (NAO>0 and NAO<0) which isb
not what i want.

ANy better ideas?

thanks and best regard,
 Stefan

messages.subject_clean: geom_ribbon and when below or above y=0
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This seems to work, but produces no legend. OTOH, neither does the NOAA plot :) If you want a legend, put the fill = 'mycolor' stuff inside aes() and add a scale_fill_manual() statement.

ggplot(nao, aes(Date, y = NAO)) +
    geom_ribbon(data = subset(nao, NAO > 0), aes(ymin = 0, ymax = NAO), fill = 'red') +
    geom_ribbon(data = subset(nao, NAO <= 0), aes(ymin = NAO, ymax = 0), fill = 'blue')

HTH,
Dennis

Try this:

nao$pos <- with(nao, pmax(0, NAO))
nao$neg <- with(nao, pmin(0, NAO))

g <- ggplot(nao, aes(x = Date))
g + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = pos), fill = 'red') +
      geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = neg, ymax = 0), fill = 'blue')

Does that work?

HTH,
Dennis

Hi Dennis,

I think it's correct. Having looked at it again, the issue I'm seeing is due to the date values all having the same day. If the data truly were daily, there'd be no issue using your solution.

But see my attachment for an illustration of how the use of monthly data, as opposed to daily, means this plot cannot look exactly as desired.

g <- ggplot(nao[nao$Year==1968,], aes(x = date))

g + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = pos), fill = 'red') +
geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = neg, ymax = 0), fill = 'blue')

See the attached.

Adam Loveland

messages.subject_clean: geom_ribbon and when below or above y=0
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

When you use geom_ribbon(), there are going to be regions of overlap if you zoom in far enough. The reason the blues and reds overlap in the subset is because there is either a single negative value in a region of positive values or vice versa, and geom_ribbon() needs to plot some area- you can see that it goes +/- 0.5 units to plot a triangle when the value is a singleton. Perhaps a viable alternative to geom_ribbon() would be geom_segment(). I'll show the code for both the full data and the subset:

url <- 'http://www.cpc.noaa.gov/products/precip/CWlink/pna/norm.nao.monthly.b5001.current.ascii'
file  <- tempfile()
download.file(url,file)
nao <- read.table(file, header = F)
names(nao) <- c('Year', 'Month', 'NAO')
nao$Date <- as.Date(paste(nao$Year, nao$Month, '15'), format = "%Y %m %d")

nao$pos <- with(nao, pmax(0, NAO))
nao$neg <- with(nao, pmin(0, NAO))

# Complete data:
q1 <- ggplot(nao, aes(x = Date))
q1 + geom_segment(aes(xend = Date, y = pos, yend = 0), color = 'red') +
     geom_segment(aes(xend = Date, y = neg, yend = 0), color = 'blue')
# On the subset:
last_plot() %+% nao2

Actually, I would probably add size = 1 to geom_segment() for visual emphasis in the latter case as follows:

ggplot(nao2, aes(x = Date)) +
   geom_segment(aes(xend = Date, y = pos, yend = 0), color = 'red', size = 1) +
   geom_segment(aes(xend = Date, y = neg, yend = 0), color = 'blue', size = 1)

You don't get the ribbon effect, but you don't get the color overlap, either. I don't see any material difference in the geom_segmented plot on the entire data frame from the geom_ribbon plot, but there is a clearly visible difference on the subset. I don't know if that's acceptable or not, but it's an alternative.

HTH,
Dennis

HI Stefan:

On Sun, Dec 19, 2010 at 7:58 AM, smu <s...@z107.de> wrote:
> Hi Dennis,
>
> On Fri, Dec 17, 2010 at 02:37:31PM -0800, Dennis Murphy wrote:
> > Hi:
> >
> > When you use geom_ribbon(), there are going to be regions of overlap if you
> > zoom in far enough. The reason the blues and reds overlap in the subset is
> > because there is either a single negative value in a region of positive
> > values or vice versa, and geom_ribbon() needs to plot some area- you can see
> > that it goes +/- 0.5 units to plot a triangle when the value is a singleton.
>
> Yes, that was my problem, I thought there could be a simple approach to
> solve, e.g. by determining, where y=0 and includes these dates in the
> data.

I don't think the problem is where y = 0; rather, it's where you get an isolated point in the series with respect to sign switch. You could use rle() to figure out where the isolated points happen to be; here's an example:

x <- rnorm(20)
# rle() is short for run length encoding - the first component, lengths,
# indicates the length of each run, whereas values tells you which value
# of the argument object corresponds to each run
> rle(x > 0)
Run Length Encoding
  lengths: int [1:11] 4 1 2 3 3 1 1 2 1 1 ...
  values : logi [1:11] FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE ...
> x
 [1] -0.41401206 -0.85060433 -1.67046027 -0.31530086  1.93378263 -0.77367688
 [7] -0.79069791  0.69257133  2.46788204  0.38892289 -0.03521033 -0.01071611
[13] -0.74209425  1.36974281 -1.22775441  0.29621976  0.28208192 -2.11044822
[19]  0.06657930 -0.18036208

To pick out the sign isolated elements of x, we do it in two stages:
      (i) select out which elements of the run length vector == 1
     (ii) make a new object that is the cumulative sum of the run lengths
    (iii) pick out the elements of the series whose components in the cumulative sum vector
          match those in (i)  [got all that? :-]
# (i)
> whichIso <- which(rle(x > 0)$lengths == 1L)
> whichIso
[1]  2  6  7  9 10 11
# (ii)
> cslengths <- cumsum(rle(x > 0)$lengths)
# (iii) Find elements of the series that are sign isolated
> x[cslengths[whichIso]]
[1]  1.9337826  1.3697428 -1.2277544 -2.1104482  0.0665793 -0.1803621

You could always try geom_ribbon() on the non-isolated set of points and then use geom_segment() on the isolated points, but I think you'll still have some localized regions of overlap between non-isolated sets. Of course, geom_ribbon() will paint over the region on the other side of the isolated point; it's up to you to decide whether that is a feature or a bug (not in the function per se, but rather its implementation).

Re geom_segment(), you can thin the width of the segments in the complete series, but it will only go so far (I think size = 0.1 or 0.05 is the practical limit from playing with it the other day). The thinned result looks pretty good, but it's not perfect because of the number of time points in the series. Some overlap of color is inherent with so many sign switches. It becomes less of a problem when the length of the series is reduced.

HTH,
Dennis

> Thank you for your suggestion of the segment plot, I think I will use
> this solution.
>
> best regards,
>  Stefan

messages.body_plain:
Hi, this may help, although not elegant:

d <- data.frame(x=rnorm(30,0,5), y=rnorm(30))
d <- d[order(d$x),] # sort along x

rx <- do.call("rbind",
  sapply(1:(nrow(d)-1), function(i){
    f <- lm(x~y, d[i:(i+1),])
    if (f$qr$rank < 2) return(NULL)
    r <- predict(f, newdata=data.frame(y=0))
    if(d[i,]$x < r & r < d[i+1,]$x)
      return(data.frame(x=r,y=0))
    else return(NULL)
  })
)
d2 <- rbind(d,rx)
ggplot(d2,aes(x,y)) + geom_point() + geom_area(data=subset(d2, y<=0),
fill="red") + geom_area(data=subset(d2, y>=0), fill="blue")

--

messages.subject_clean: how to use spline() with ggplot?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dennis,

Thank you for your help, but these approaches  uses a smoothed spline
and I would like to fit a spline through all of the points.

In addition, I am using the spline() function for my analysis so it
would definitely be preferable to use spline() instead of rcs() or
ns().

Do you know how I can incorporate spline() into ggplot?

Thanks,

David

On Nov 29, 9:04 pm, Dennis Murphy <djmu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> Here's an example:
>
> x = seq(0, 2 * pi, length = 500)
> df <- data.frame(x = x, y = sin(x) + rnorm(500, s = 0.3))
>
> library(splines)
> ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
>      stat_smooth(data = g, aes(x = x, y = y), method = 'lm',
>                           formula = y ~ ns(x, 3), col = 'red', size = 2, se=
> FALSE)
>
> It should be simpler if you use lm() with one of the spline functions
> generating the basis matrix. I used ns() here, but one could use other basis
> functions equally well. Here's a different example using the rcs() function
> in package rms:
>
> library(rms)
> ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
>      stat_smooth(data = g, aes(x = x, y = y), method = 'lm',
>                           formula = y ~ rcs(x, 4), col = 'red', size = 2,
> se= FALSE)
>
> The graph should be essentially the same. The se argument is unneeded
> because confidence curves won't be plotted if you specify se = TRUE.
>
> HTH,
> Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Adding legend to geom_rect()
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Try this:

df<-data.frame(x=c(1:5), y1=c(1:5),y2=c(8:12))
df2 <- melt(df, id = 'x')
names(df2) <- c('x', 'var', 'y')
ggplot(df2, aes(xmin=x,xmax=x+1)) +
  geom_rect(aes(ymin=y, ymax=y+1, fill= var)) +
  scale_fill_manual("", breaks = levels(df2$var),
                        values = c('blue', 'red'),
                        labels = c('Series 1', 'Series 2'))

(1) I melted the data to create a factor variable that can distinguish the two sets of y's
(2) The renamed factor is 'var', which you can map to fill in geom_rect()
(3) The empty double quote at the beginning of the scale call => no legend title. You can always fill one in.

Legends are very tricky for novices - I had a hard time with them for a few months. Scales are associated with mapped aesthetics (i.e., aesthetic elements that are set to variables inside aes() rather than constants). The scale_* functions let you manipulate aspects of the scale. Since the labels you want are different from the variable names and specific colors are desired, the most convenient thing to do in this case is to construct a manual scale, which provides the most control over features of the legend (and the most frustration :). The breaks are identified with the levels of the fill variable, the values = part associates colors with each level in breaks (in order), and labels = does the same for text labels. Also notice that the manual scale is associated with fill by name (scale_fill_manual).

> On Mon, Dec 20, 2010 at 1:35 AM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > HI Stefan:
> >
> > On Sun, Dec 19, 2010 at 7:58 AM, smu <s...@z107.de> wrote:
> >>
> >> Hi Dennis,
> >>
> >> On Fri, Dec 17, 2010 at 02:37:31PM -0800, Dennis Murphy wrote:
> >> > Hi:
> >> >
> >> > When you use geom_ribbon(), there are going to be regions of overlap if
> >> > you
> >> > zoom in far enough. The reason the blues and reds overlap in the subset
> >> > is
> >> > because there is either a single negative value in a region of positive
> >> > values or vice versa, and geom_ribbon() needs to plot some area- you can
> >> > see
> >> > that it goes +/- 0.5 units to plot a triangle when the value is a
> >> > singleton.
> >>
> >> Yes, that was my problem, I thought there could be a simple approach to
> >> solve, e.g. by determining, where y=0 and includes these dates in the
> >> data.
> >
> > I don't think the problem is where y = 0; rather, it's where you get an
> > isolated point in the series with respect to sign switch. You could use
> > rle() to figure out where the isolated points happen to be; here's an
> > example:
> >
> > x <- rnorm(20)
> > # rle() is short for run length encoding - the first component, lengths,
> > # indicates the length of each run, whereas values tells you which value
> > # of the argument object corresponds to each run
> >> rle(x > 0)
> > Run Length Encoding
> > � lengths: int [1:11] 4 1 2 3 3 1 1 2 1 1 ...
> > � values : logi [1:11] FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE ...
> >> x
> > �[1] -0.41401206 -0.85060433 -1.67046027 -0.31530086� 1.93378263 -0.77367688
> > �[7] -0.79069791� 0.69257133� 2.46788204� 0.38892289 -0.03521033 -0.01071611
> > [13] -0.74209425� 1.36974281 -1.22775441� 0.29621976� 0.28208192 -2.11044822
> > [19]� 0.06657930 -0.18036208
> >
> > To pick out the sign isolated elements of x, we do it in two stages:
> > ����� (i) select out which elements of the run length vector == 1
> > ���� (ii) make a new object that is the cumulative sum of the run lengths
> > ��� (iii) pick out the elements of the series whose components in the
> > cumulative sum vector
> > ��������� match those in (i)� [got all that? :-]
> > # (i)
> >> whichIso <- which(rle(x > 0)$lengths == 1L)
> >> whichIso
> > [1]� 2� 6� 7� 9 10 11
> > # (ii)
> >> cslengths <- cumsum(rle(x > 0)$lengths)
> > # (iii) Find elements of the series that are sign isolated
> >> x[cslengths[whichIso]]
> > [1]� 1.9337826� 1.3697428 -1.2277544 -2.1104482� 0.0665793 -0.1803621
> >
> > You could always try geom_ribbon() on the non-isolated set of points and
> > then use geom_segment() on the isolated points, but I think you'll still
> > have some localized regions of overlap between non-isolated sets. Of course,
> > geom_ribbon() will paint over the region on the other side of the isolated
> > point; it's up to you to decide whether that is a feature or a bug (not in
> > the function per se, but rather its implementation).
> >
> > Re geom_segment(), you can thin the width of the segments in the complete
> > series, but it will only go so far (I think size = 0.1 or 0.05 is the
> > practical limit from playing with it the other day). The thinned result
> > looks pretty good, but it's not perfect because of the number of time points
> > in the series. Some overlap of color is inherent with so many sign switches.
> > It becomes less of a problem when the length of the series is reduced.
> >
> > HTH,
> > Dennis

> >> this solution.

messages.subject: Cropping of axis labels
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

When I manually assign labels to an axis scale, long strings are cropped
at the edge of the plot area and thus only partially visible:

----
d <- data.frame(x=c(1:4), y=(1:4),
                labels=c('Dear Hadley', 'could you fix this', 'before Christmas,',
                  'pretty pretty please with lots of cropping on top?'))

ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=d$x, labels=d$labels) +
  opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(size=12, angle=-35, hjust=0))
----

I was able to work around this by adjusting plot.margin via opts(),
which works but is a bit tedious. So I thought I'd flag this in case
it's a bug or, if it is not, to ask whether there is a better way of
dealing with the problem.

Thanks,
Christian

messages.subject_clean: how to use spline() with ggplot?
messages.body_plain:
>From the help page of spline():

spline returns a list containing components x and y which give the ordinates where interpolation took place and the interpolated values.

Take the results from spline(), assign them to an object, convert it to a data frame and use that as input into ggplot(), where you can use either geom_path() or geom_line() to produce the plot.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Cropping of axis labels
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Wed, Dec 22, 2010 at 4:48 AM, Christian Kreibich <chri...@icir.org> wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> When I manually assign labels to an axis scale, long strings are cropped
> at the edge of the plot area and thus only partially visible:
>
> ----
> d <- data.frame(x=c(1:4), y=(1:4),
>                labels=c('Dear Hadley', 'could you fix this', 'before Christmas,',
>                  'pretty pretty please with lots of cropping on top?'))
>
> ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
>  scale_x_continuous(breaks=d$x, labels=d$labels) +
>  opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(size=12, angle=-35, hjust=0))
> ----
>
> I was able to work around this by adjusting plot.margin via opts(),
> which works but is a bit tedious. So I thought I'd flag this in case
> it's a bug or, if it is not, to ask whether there is a better way of
> dealing with the problem.

(a) Use a 90 degree angle - that would avoid the cropping problem (at least to the right).
(b) Use a less severe angle.
(c) Rotate the graph axis so that someone can more easily read the labels.
(d) Put line breaks in your labels to avoid overly long strings.
(e) Reduce the size of the text font.
etc.

Long labels are almost always better placed on the y-axis rather than the x-axis.

My opinion is this is a graphics design issue which doesn't require a software rewrite to solve. In my experience, if you need to insert long lines to annotate a graphic, you need to rethink how to construct your graphic. The more graphics space one assigns to the margins, the less area one has available for the actual graphic (not to mention the impact on the aspect ratio). If this is meant to go inside a document, you can use the caption for annotation or provide additional explanation in the text. For example, I almost never put titles on graphs that go in documents any more; I use the caption for that purpose.

Just my 2 pfennig.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Adding legend to geom_rect()
messages.body_plain:
> Legends are very tricky for novices - I had a hard time with them for a few
> months. Scales are associated with mapped aesthetics (i.e., aesthetic
> elements that are set to variables inside aes() rather than constants). The
> scale_* functions let you manipulate aspects of the scale. Since the labels
> you want are different from the variable names and specific colors are
> desired, the most convenient thing to do in this case is to construct a
> manual scale, which provides the most control over features of the legend
> (and the most frustration :). The breaks are identified with the levels of
> the fill variable, the values = part associates colors with each level in
> breaks (in order), and labels = does the same for text labels. Also notice
> that the manual scale is associated with fill by name (scale_fill_manual).

My advice is to always think about the data - what variable are you
mapping to the fill colour? If that variable doesn't exist in your
data, it may be suggesting that you should reshape the data so that it
is.

Hadley

Hi:

This gets rid of the ticks on both the x- and y- axis. I'll let you decide whether or not it's acceptable.

... + opts(axis.ticks = theme_blank())

As far as I can tell from the book documentation, it's not possible to remove the ticks on one axis at present...but perhaps someone will show you that/how it can be done. (I'm aware of ongoing work to separate tasks, so it may well be available in the foreseeable future.) Lattice and base graphics allow this type of separation of tasks, however, if it's that important.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: ggplot2 0.8.9 - Merry Christmas version
messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot2 is a plotting system for R, based on the grammar of graphics,
which tries to take the good parts of base and lattice graphics and
avoid bad parts. It takes care of many of the fiddly details
that make plotting a hassle (like drawing legends) as well as
providing a powerful model of graphics that makes it easy to produce
complex multi-layered graphics.

To install or update, run:
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "plyr"))

Find out more at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2, and check out the nearly 500
examples of ggplot in use.  If you're interested, you can also sign up to
the ggplot2 mailing list at http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2, or track
development at  http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2

ggplot2 0.8.9 (2010-12-24) ----------------------------------------

A big thanks to Koshke Takahashi, who supplied the majority of
improvements in this release!

GUIDE IMPROVEMENTS

* key size: can specify width and height separately

* axis: can partially handle text rotation (issue #149)

* legend: now can specify the direction of element by opts(legend.direction =
  "vertical") or opts(legend.direction = "horizontal"), and legend box is
  center aligned if horizontal

* legend: now can override the alignment of legend box by
  opts(legend.box = "vertical") or opts(legend.box = "horizontal")

* legend: now can override legend title alignment with opts(legend.title.align
  = 0) or opts(legend.title.align = 1)

* legend: can override legend text alignment with opts(legend.text.align = 0)
  or opts(legend.text.align = 1)

BUG FIXES

* theme_*: can specify font-family for all text elements other than geom_text

* facet_grid: fixed hirozontal spacing when nrow of horizontal strip >= 2

* facet_grid: now can manually specify the relative size of each row and column

* is.zero: now correctly works

* +: adding NULL to a plot returns the plot (idempotent under addition)
  (thanks to suggestion by Matthew O'Meara)

* +: meaningful error message if + doesn't know how to deal with an object
  type

* coord_cartesian and coord_flip: now can wisely zoom when wise = TRUE

* coord_polar: fix point division bugs

* facet_grid: now labels in facet_grid are correctly aligned when the number
  of factors is more then one (fixes #87 and #65)

* geom_hex: now correctly applies alpha to fill colour not outline colour
  (thanks to bug report from Ian Fellows)

* geom_polygon: specifying linetype now works (thanks to fix from Kohske
  Takahashi)

* hcl: can now set c and l, and preserves names (thanks to suggestion by
  Richard Cotton)

* mean_se: a new summary function to work with stat_summary that calculates
  mean and one standard error on either side (thanks to contribution from
  Kohske Takahashi)

* pos_stack: now works with NAs in x

* scale_alpha: setting limits to a range inside the data now works (thanks to
  report by Dr Proteome)

* scale_colour_continuous: works correctly with single continuous value (fixes
  #73)

* scale_identity: now show legends (fix #119)

* stat_function: now works without y values

* stat_smooth: draw line if only 2 unique x values, not three as previously *
  guides: fixed #126

* stat_smooth: once again works if n > 1000 and SE = F (thanks to bug report
  from Theiry Onkelinx and fix from Kohske Takahashi)

* stat_smooth: works with locfit (fix #129)

* theme_text handles alignment better when angle = 90

--
Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
Department of Statistics / Rice University

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Using this code, I get inconsistent justification of the x axis text
--- the left facet is correctly justified but the right facet isn't:

d <- data.frame(a=rnorm(100),
b=factor(sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 100, TRUE)),
c=factor(sample(c("1", "2"), 100, TRUE)))

d2 <- d[d$c == "1" | (d$c == "2" & d$b == "C"),]

ggplot(d2, aes(x=b, y=a)) + facet_grid(~ c, space="free",
scales="free") + geom_point() + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=90,
hjust=1))

compare with

ggplot(d2, aes(x=b, y=a)) + facet_grid(~ c, space="free") +
geom_point() + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=90, hjust=1))

Is this a bug?

Thanks,
Gad

Hi, now I figure out that this is due to the recent modification.
If you use only the combination of angle = 90 and hjust = 1, then
ggplot-0.8.8 works better.
So, put code below before calling ggplot2:

== from here ==
guide_axis <- function(at, labels, position="right", theme) {
  position <- match.arg(position, c("top", "bottom", "right", "left"))

  at <- unit(at, "native")
  length <- theme$axis.ticks.length
  label_pos <- length + theme$axis.ticks.margin
  one <- unit(1, "npc")

  label_render <- switch(position,
    top = , bottom = "axis.text.x",
    left = , right = "axis.text.y"
  )
  label_x <- switch(position,
    top = ,
    bottom = at,
    right = label_pos,
    left = one - label_pos
  )
  label_y <- switch(position,
    top = label_pos,
    bottom = one - label_pos,
    right = ,
    left = at,
  )

  if (is.list(labels)) {
    if (any(sapply(labels, is.language))) {
      labels <- do.call(expression, labels)
    } else {
      labels <- unlist(labels)
    }
  }

  labels <- theme_render(theme, label_render, labels, label_x, label_y)

  line <- switch(position,
    top =    theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 0, 1, 0),
    bottom = theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 1, 1, 1),
    right =  theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 1, 0, 1),
    left =   theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 1, 0, 1, 1)
  )

  ticks <- switch(position,
    top =    theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", at, 0, at, length),
    bottom = theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", at, one - length, at, 1),
    right =  theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", 0, at, length, at),
    left =   theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", one - length, at, 1, at)
  )

  absoluteGrob(
    gList(ticks, labels, line),
    width = grobWidth(labels) + label_pos,
    height = grobHeight(labels) + label_pos
  )
}
assignInNamespace("guide_axis",guide_axis, "ggplot2")

== to here ==

Note that if you want to use hjust 0 with angle = 90, then ggplot2 can
correctly handle, for example, try these in ggplot2-0.8.8 (i.e., but

2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 3L), .Label = c("x1", "x2", "y1"), class = "factor"),
    value = c(10L, 11L, 13L, 18L, 19L, 21L, 123L, 124L, 130L),
    facet.var = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L)), .Names = c("year",
"variable", "value", "facet.var"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA,
-9L))

ggplot(data=data, aes(year, value, colour=variable))+geom_line()

I can see why you want to use another scale for your data. The y data for the one variable is 1 log10 higher than the other.

I'm pretty sure there is still no way within ggplot to have more than one axis scale, and I believe that this is because it is quite difficult, but perhaps more importantly, it is very misleading. One way around this could be to plot the x's and the y's as two plots independently and then put them next to each other. I'd love to be wrong here since there have been times where two scales would have been useful.

-B

Hi:

Re the multiple graphics scales on one axis, see

http://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/How-to-change-the-default-location-of-x-axis-in-ggplot2-td3161204.html

particularly Hadley's response.

On Mon, Dec 27, 2010 at 2:38 AM, SNV Krishna <kri...@primps.com.sg> wrote:
> Dear All,
>
> Is it possible to have multiple lines on leftside y-axis and right side y-axis in ggplot2. I assume there is a way but do not know how to accomplish it. For ex. the data set looks like this
>
> year variable value
> 2007 x1 10
> 2008 x1 11
> 2009 x1 13
> 2007 x2 18
> 2008 x2 19
> 2009 x2 21
> 2007 y1 123
> 2008 y1 124
> 2009 y1 130
>
> I would like to get a line plot of x1 and x2 against year on left hand side y-axis and y1 on right hand side y-axis. any help or ideas will be greatly appreciated.

The approach to which Brandon alluded is sensible; i.e., a conditioning plot by variable with free ranging y-scales. Something like (untested, and assuming your data frame is named df)

ggplot(df, aes(x = year, y = value)) + geom_line(aes(group = variable)) + facet_grid(. ~ variable, scales = 'free_y')

[Replace group with color or linetype if you want to identify the individual series in a legend.] If you want the first two in the same panel, you could do something like

df$var <- factor(substr(as.character(df$variable), 1, 1))     # should end up with x and y as levels
ggplot(df, aes(x = year, y = value)) + geom_line(aes(group = variable)) +
       facet_grid(var ~ ., scales = 'free_y')

To get the y plot on top, which would make more sense to me, reverse the levels in df$var:
df$var <- factor(substr(as.character(df$variable), 1, 1), levels = c('y', 'x'))

and repeat the above ggplot() + ... line.

There are graphics tricks you can pull if you want (some of them are in the plotrix package and used in conjunction with base graphics), but since I don't endorse any of them, you're on your own if you want to go in that direction.

HTH,
Dennis

http://dl.dropbox.com/u/15384925/Economic%20Indicators.pdf

undefined columns, variables not found in the molten data etc).

Very grateful for any help

Simeon

########################
###

library(ggplot2)
data(economics)

adGraphData <- function(data,period,indicator1,indicator2) {
    df <- melt(data,id=period,measure=c(indicator1,indicator2))
    df$panel <- "ind1"
    df[df$variable %in% indicator2,"panel"] <- "ind2"
    df$panel <- factor(df$panel,levels=c("ind1","ind2"),ordered=T)
    df
}

adGraph <- function(data,period,indicator1,indicator2,...){
    df <-
adGraphData(data=data,period=period,indicator1=indicator1,indicator2=indicator2)
    p  <- ggplot(df,aes_string(period,"value"))
    p + geom_line()
    p +  geom_line(subset=.(panel=="ind1"),aes(colour=factor(df
$variable)),size=1.2)+
         geom_smooth(subset=.(panel=="ind1"),size=1)+
         geom_area(subset=.(panel=="ind2"),aes(fill=factor(df
$variable)),alpha=0.6)+
         scale_y_continuous("",formatter=comma)+
         scale_colour_grey("Ind1") +
scale_fill_brewer("Ind2",palette="Set1")+
         facet_grid(df$panel ~. ,heights=c(2,1),scales="free")

}

messages.subject: scale_fill_brewer problem with continuous data
messages.body_plain:
I was working on a geom_tile() plot and could not get
scale_fill_brewer to work.

I started with . . .

scale_fill_continuous( "", limits= c( 0, 100), low= "yellow", high=
"green")

. . . and got approximately what I wanted but the palette wasn't quite
right.

When I added . . .

scale_fill_brewer( "", palette="YlGn", limits= c( 0,100), breaks=
seq(0,100,by=20))

. . . I got two colors that appear to be from the middle of the
palette mapped to the limits and no fills for the intermediate values.

To get it to work I had to write . . .

seqTheme <- colorRampPalette( brewer.pal( 5, "YlGn"),
                             space="Lab")

. . . and then add to my plot . . .

scale_fill_gradientn( colours= seqTheme( 5),
                     limits= c( 0, 100),
                     breaks= seq( 0, 100, by= 20))

Is this a bug or am I doing something wrong?  Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: scale_fill_brewer problem with continuous data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Probably scale_fill_brewer and scale_colour_brewer are designed to use
with categorical (i.e., discrete) variable.

scale_fill_gradientn() is suitable, and you can do it simply by

p <- ggplot(data.frame(x=0:100, y=0), aes(x, y, fill=x)) + geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours=brewer.pal(7,"YlGn"))

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html

messages.subject: Re: Functions & variable names
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

My interpretation of the original question was how to pass the value of period declared in the function call into aes_string(). My first thought was substitute(), but I couldn't figure out  the right mantra so I tried bquote() instead.

Here's my tweak on Brandon's modification:

# ---------------

adGraph <- function(data, period, indicator1, indicator2,...){

# Reshape the input data frame
df <- melt(data, id=period, measure=c(indicator1, indicator2))

   df$panel <- "ind1"
   df[df$variable %in% indicator2,"panel"] <- "ind2"
   df$panel <- factor(df$panel, levels=c("ind1","ind2"), ordered=T)

# Create the plot - pass value of period into aes_string() via bquote()
p<-ggplot(df, aes_string(x = bquote(.(period)), y = "value")) + geom_line() +

        geom_line(subset=.(panel=="ind1"),
                aes_string(colour="factor(variable)"), size = 1.2) +
        geom_smooth(subset=.(panel=="ind1"),size=1) +
        geom_area(subset=.(panel=="ind2"),
                  aes_string(fill="factor(variable)"), alpha=0.6) +
        scale_y_continuous("", formatter=comma) +
        scale_colour_grey("Ind1") +
        scale_fill_brewer("Ind2", palette="Set1")+

        facet_grid(panel ~ . , heights=c(2,1), scales="free_y")

print(p)
   }

adGraph(data=economics, period="date", indicator1="unemploy", indicator2=c("psavert", "uempmed"))

# ------------------
AFAICT, it yields the same plot as Brandon's solution and should be a little more general.

The warning is simply to state that scale_*_brewer() uses a minimum of three and a maximum of eight colors in the palette. I'm not quite sure of what's going on in the area plot, but I haven't looked at the data frame that closely and don't have much occasion to use area plots. It appears that the bottom panel is of the contemporaneous time series of psavert (whose minimum value is negative) and uempmed. The area plot looks nice, but the shadings from pink to dark red and from light to dark blue (not to mention the little section of black at the end) isn't represented in the legend so it kind of begs the question as to what it's supposed to represent...I'm guessing overlap of one series onto the other in combination with the alpha transparency, but it's not obvious, which means some explanation is likely to be necessary if the graph goes in a report as shown.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
I guess when it is trying to define the x and y axis it is using the a and b from the aes() call in the ggplot() call as reference, but when you then use a different data for your geom_rect() layer it doesn't know what to do.

If you switch df2 and df1 like below the code works without error so it is clearly the lack of an a and b value in your df2 dataframe. That being said, geom_rect() does not require an x or y in the aes() call as you noted. It does seem slightly inconsistent but easily avoidable.

df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)

ggplot(data = df2, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
               data = df1,

               xmin = 0,
               xmax = 1,
               ymin = 0,
               ymax = 1)

I think the more important question would be why are you wanting to reference one dataframe and then supply geom_rect() another? If you have more than one dataframe to reference then you will likely have another layer to plot. Best thing to do is to supply each layer individually with "data=df, aes(x=x, y=y,...)" to avoid confusion for you and the program.

HTH,

Brandon

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I see that in the second case you are calling a different data frame than that mapped to the aesthetic. Geom_rect needs an aesthetic and you've specified it to have x=a, yet to use df2, when df2 does not have variable "a". Since you are doing nothing with a, b, aa and bb:

ggplot(data=df2) + geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0,

                xmax = 1,
                ymin = 0,

                ymax = 1))

or map the variables...

ggplot(data=df2) + geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0,
                xmax = aa,              #use a if using df1, etc.
                ymin = 0,
                ymax = bb))

or to look like your first case, but doing nothing with df1 and the first aesthetic...

df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
                data = df2,

                   aes(x=aa, y=bb),

                xmin = 0,
                xmax = 1,
                ymin = 0,
                ymax = 1)

or...

df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
                data = df2,

                   aes(x=aa,
                   y=bb,

                xmin = 0,
                xmax = 1,
                ymin = 0,

                ymax = 1))

HTH

/Leo
